## 1. Cash basis for the self-employed (HIGH BLAST RADIUS, 5 pages)

### 1.1 Thresholds: ABOLISHED, not raised

**Locked position.** There are **no turnover entry or exit thresholds for the income tax cash basis** from 2024/25 onward. The old £150,000 entry / £300,000 exit limits were **repealed outright**, not increased. Eligibility now turns solely on **who** you are (sole trader or partnership without corporate partners) and whether the trade is an **excluded trade**, never on turnover.

- **Source:** *Income Tax (Trading and Other Income) Act 2005*, **s.25A "Cash basis for small businesses"**, text now reading ". . . . . . ."; amendment note: **omitted (6.4.2024 for the tax year 2024-25 and subsequent tax years) by Finance Act 2024 (c. 3), Sch. 10 paras. 4, 47** (transitionals paras. 48-50). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/5/section/25A
- **Source:** *Finance Act 2024*, **Schedule 10** (para. 6 omits the ss.31A-31D turnover-condition provisions; para. 47 commencement "The amendments made by this Schedule have effect for the tax year 2024-25 and subsequent tax years"). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2024/3/schedule/10
- **Source:** gov.uk, *Cash basis: Who can use cash basis* - "You can use cash basis if you're a sole trader or partnership without corporate partners." No turnover figure appears anywhere on the eligibility page. https://www.gov.uk/simpler-income-tax-cash-basis/who-can-use-cash-basis

**Confidence: LOCKED.** *This is the fact typical summaries get wrong: most say the threshold "was raised to £300,000" or "£1.35m". Both are wrong. The thresholds were removed entirely.*

### 1.2 Default status and how to opt out

**Locked position.** The cash basis is the **default** for eligible unincorporated businesses. A business leaves it by making a **positive election** for profits to be calculated under GAAP (what gov.uk calls "traditional accounting"); the election has effect for the year made and subsequent years until revoked or the trade becomes excluded.

- **Source:** *ITTOIA 2005 s.24A "Cash basis to apply by default"* (inserted by FA 2024 Sch. 10 paras. 2, 47, in force 6.4.2024 for 2024-25 onward): "**(1) The profits of a trade for a tax year must be calculated on the cash basis, unless - (a) the trade is an excluded trade in relation to the tax year (see section 25B), or (b) an election under section 25C(1) has effect in relation to the trade for the tax year.**" Also s.24A(4): where the cash basis applies, ss.27, 28 and 30 do not apply. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/5/section/24A
- **Source:** *ITTOIA 2005 s.25C* (election for profits to be calculated in accordance with GAAP). https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/5/section/25C
- **Source:** gov.uk cash basis: "When you send your Self Assessment tax return you'll need to say that you've used traditional accounting." https://www.gov.uk/simpler-income-tax-cash-basis/who-can-use-cash-basis

**Confidence: LOCKED.** Caveat: the **time limit** for the s.25C election is not stated on the s.25C page itself and was not separately verified. Pages must not assert a specific election deadline; say "elect on the return" and stop.

### 1.3 Interest deductibility

**Locked position.** The **£500 cap on interest deductions under the cash basis has been abolished**. Interest and finance costs are now deductible under the ordinary wholly-and-exclusively rules, the same as on the accruals basis.

- **Source:** *ITTOIA 2005 s.51A "Cash basis: interest payments on loans"*, text omitted; note: "omitted (6.4.2024 for the tax year 2024-25 and subsequent tax years) by Finance Act 2024 (c. 3), Sch. 10 paras. 7(a), 47". https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/5/section/51A

**Confidence: LOCKED.**

### 1.4 Loss relief (sideways relief)

**Locked position.** The bar on sideways and carry-back loss relief for cash basis losses has been **removed**. A cash basis trading loss now qualifies for the ordinary loss reliefs (sideways against general income, carry-back, terminal), subject to the general loss-relief rules and caps.

- **Source:** *Income Tax Act 2007 s.74E "No relief where cash basis used to calculate losses"*, text omitted; note: "S. 74E and cross-heading omitted (6.4.2024 for the tax year 2024-25 and subsequent tax years) by virtue of Finance Act 2024 (c. 3), Sch. 10 paras. 8(a), 47". https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2007/3/section/74E

**Confidence: LOCKED.**

### 1.5 Capital allowances under the cash basis

**Locked position.** On the cash basis, **capital allowances are switched off except for cars**. Capital expenditure is instead deducted as an ordinary expense when paid, unless it falls in the s.33A excluded list (notably **cars**, land, buildings, financial assets, intangibles, and expenditure on acquiring or disposing of a business). So there is **no AIA** on the cash basis; a car remains in the capital allowances regime (WDA by CO2, per §8 of house_positions).

- **Source:** *Capital Allowances Act 2001 s.1A*: "The person is not entitled to any allowance or liable to any charge under this Act except as provided by subsections (4) and (7)"; the carve-out at (4): "If, apart from subsection (2), the person would be entitled to an allowance in respect of expenditure incurred on the provision of **a car** ... the person is so entitled". https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2001/2/section/1A
- **Source:** *ITTOIA 2005 s.33A "Cash basis: capital expenditure"*: no deduction for capital items "incurred on, or in connection with, the acquisition or disposal of a business or part of a business", nor for "**a car (see subsection (14))**" (car taking its Part 2 CAA 2001 meaning), land, non-depreciating assets, financial assets, non-qualifying intangibles. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/5/section/33A

**Confidence: LOCKED.** Writing rule: never say "claim AIA on the cash basis". Say the cost is deducted as an expense when paid, and cars are the exception that stays in capital allowances.

### 1.6 Limited companies

**Locked position.** The income tax cash basis is **not available to limited companies**, and never has been. It is a rule in ITTOIA 2005 Part 2, which charges **income tax** on the trading profits of individuals and partnerships. A company's profits are computed under **CTA 2009 s.46(1)**, which mandates GAAP. This is a completely different thing from the **VAT Cash Accounting Scheme** (§2 below), which a company *can* use.

- **Source:** *ITTOIA 2005 s.24A(1)* (applies to "the profits of a trade for a tax year", income tax) https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/5/section/24A ; gov.uk cash basis: "Some businesses cannot use cash basis, for example, limited companies", and the eligibility list bars "limited company", "limited liability partnership", "partnership with one or more corporate partners". https://www.gov.uk/simpler-income-tax-cash-basis and https://www.gov.uk/simpler-income-tax-cash-basis/who-can-use-cash-basis

**Confidence: LOCKED.** Consistent with house_positions §21.8.5, which already says "limited companies cannot use it".

### 1.7 Cross-check against house_positions.md

- §21.8.5 states the cash basis "is the **default from 2024/25**, with an election out into accruals, and **limited companies cannot use it**". **CONFIRMED, no change needed.**
- §21.8 open question (3) says: "**Do not cite ITTOIA 2005 ss.31A to 31D as the live cash-basis provisions** ... the *section numbers* must be pinned to the post-FA 2024 text before any page cites them." **NOW RESOLVED.** The live provisions are **ITTOIA 2005 ss.24A (default), 25B (excluded trades), 25C (election out), 33A (capital expenditure)**, plus **CAA 2001 s.1A**. ss.25A, 31A-31D, 51A and ITA 2007 s.74E are all omitted from 6.4.2024. This open question can be closed at the lock gate.
- **BIM70010 is STALE.** Fetched 2026-09-11: it still frames the cash basis as an election and still states the "£150,000 threshold for 2017-18 onwards". https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/business-income-manual/bim70010 - **do not cite BIM70010 for cash basis eligibility on any page.** Cite the statute.

## 2. VAT Cash Accounting Scheme (a DIFFERENT thing, thresholds still exist)

**Locked position.** Join the VAT Cash Accounting Scheme if **estimated VAT taxable turnover is £1.35 million or less** in the next 12 months; you must **leave once VAT taxable turnover exceeds £1.6 million**. These thresholds are alive and unchanged. **Contrast for the `vat-cash-basis-threshold` page:** the *VAT* scheme has thresholds and is open to limited companies; the *income tax* cash basis has **no thresholds at all** and is **closed** to limited companies. They share only a name.

- **Source:** gov.uk, *Cash Accounting Scheme: Eligibility* - join where "your estimated VAT taxable turnover is £1.35 million or less in the next 12 months"; leave where "your VAT taxable turnover is more than £1.6 million". https://www.gov.uk/vat-cash-accounting-scheme/eligibility

**Confidence: LOCKED. Agrees with house_positions §7** ("join if taxable turnover is £1.35 million or less, leave when it exceeds £1.6 million"). No contradiction.

## 3. Terminology: "accruals basis" vs GAAP

**Locked position.** HMRC's consumer-facing name for the non-cash basis is **"traditional accounting (accruals basis)"**; the statutory name is **"generally accepted accounting practice"**. All three are HMRC's own words, so "accruals basis" is safe in copy provided the statutory hook cited is GAAP.

- **Source:** HMRC helpsheet **HS222 "How to calculate your taxable profits"** - "cash basis accounting - you record income when you get it and expenses when you pay them"; "**traditional accounting (accruals basis)** - you record income when you invoice your customers and expenses when you receive a bill". https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/how-to-calculate-your-taxable-profits-hs222-self-assessment-helpsheet/hs222-how-to-calculate-your-taxable-profits-2025
- **Source:** *ITTOIA 2005 s.25(1)*: "The profits of a trade to which the cash basis does not apply must be calculated in accordance with **generally accepted accounting practice**, subject to any adjustment required or authorised by law in calculating profits for income tax purposes." https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/5/section/25

**Confidence: LOCKED.** Matches house_positions §21.8.1 verbatim.

## 4. Motor (HIGH BLAST RADIUS, 4 pages)

### 4.1 The input tax block on cars

**Locked position.** VAT on the purchase (or hire) of a **motor car** is **blocked** from input tax credit. The block is lifted only where the car is a **qualifying motor car** intended for one of the listed uses: **stock in trade** of a manufacturer or dealer (unused cars), **letting on hire**, **taxi / hire with a driver for carrying passengers**, **self-drive hire**, **driving instruction**, conversion, or manufacturer R&D, or where the car is intended to be used **exclusively for the purposes of the business**.

**The availability trap:** intending to make the car available for anyone's private use, for consideration or not, **defeats** the "exclusively for business" test outright. Merely not using it privately is not enough; there must be nothing permitting private use.

- **Source:** *Value Added Tax (Input Tax) Order 1992 (SI 1992/3222), **article 7***, latest available revised text. Art. 7(1): "tax charged on the supply (including a letting on hire) to a taxable person ... of a motor car shall be **excluded from any credit** under section 25 of the Act." Art. 7(2): exceptions for a "qualifying motor car", dealer stock, letting on hire, unused cars to lessors for passenger transport. Art. 7(2E)/(2F): qualifying uses = hire with driver for carrying passengers, self-drive hire (broadly under 30 consecutive days, under 90 days in 12 months), driving instruction. **Art. 7(2G): "A taxable person shall not be taken to intend to use a motor car exclusively for the purposes of a business carried on by him if he intends to let it on hire for inadequate consideration or make it available to any person for private use, whether or not for consideration."** https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1992/3222/article/7
- **Source (definition of "car"):** *Motoring expenses (VAT Notice 700/64)* - "A car for VAT purposes is any motor vehicle of a kind normally used on public roads, which has 3 or more wheels and either: is constructed or adapted mainly for carrying passengers [or] has roofed accommodation to the rear of driver's seat that's fitted with side windows". **Not cars:** vehicles accommodating only one person or 12+ including the driver; caravans, ambulances, prison vans; vehicles of not less than 3 tonnes unladen; special purpose vehicles (ice cream vans, mobile shops, hearses, bullion vans, breakdown/recovery); **vehicles with a payload of one tonne or more**. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/vat-on-motoring-expenses-notice-70064
- **Source (the test in HMRC's words):** same Notice - "A car is used exclusively for business purposes if you use it only for business journeys and it is not available for private use. This means that you do not intend to make it available for the private use of employees or anyone else." And: "A car is available for private use when there's nothing preventing you or your employee from using the car for private use."

**Confidence: LOCKED.** Note the **one-tonne payload** line is what takes most double-cab pickups and van-derived vehicles out of the VAT car definition; do not conflate this with the separate ITEPA benefit-in-kind classification, which changed for double-cab pickups from April 2025 and was **not verified here**.

### 4.2 Second-hand margin scheme for vehicles

**Locked position.** A dealer buying a used vehicle **without VAT on the invoice** may account for output VAT on the **margin only**, computed as **1/6 of the gross margin** (selling price minus purchase price). Where the sale price is at or below the purchase price there is no VAT. Conditions are record-driven: normal VAT records **plus a stock book tracking each vehicle individually**, plus purchase and sales invoices both ways. **You cannot reclaim input tax on a margin scheme purchase** (there is none to reclaim, and the scheme is unavailable for any vehicle bought on an invoice showing VAT separately), and **you must not show VAT separately on a margin scheme sales invoice** (so the buyer cannot recover any either).

- **Source:** gov.uk, *Using the VAT margin scheme for second-hand vehicles* - "multiply the gross margin by **1/6**"; "You must keep normal VAT records when you use the margin scheme" plus "a stock book that tracks each item sold under the margin scheme individually" and "copies of purchase and sales invoices for all items"; scheme unavailable for "any vehicle purchased on an invoice which shows VAT separately"; VAT must not be shown separately on the sales invoice. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/using-the-vat-margin-scheme-for-second-hand-vehicles
- **Source:** gov.uk, *Buying second-hand vehicles using a VAT margin scheme* - "Get a purchase invoice and enter the details in your stock book." https://www.gov.uk/guidance/buying-second-hand-vehicles-using-a-vat-margin-scheme

**Confidence: LOCKED.** Agrees with house_positions §21.1 (one-sixth of the margin, stock book constitutive, margin lost item-by-item on records). **Note for the writing rule:** VAT Notice 718/1 is now marked **[Withdrawn]** on gov.uk and has been replaced by the three "second-hand vehicles margin scheme" guidance pages; **cite the live pages, not 718/1**. House_positions §21.1 and its authority anchors cite Notices 718 and 718/1 - that citation is stale and should be re-pointed at the lock gate (the substance is unchanged).

### 4.3 Leased cars: the 50% restriction

**Locked position.** Where a qualifying car is **leased** and is available for any private use, only **50% of the VAT on the lease charge** is recoverable. The 50% block applies to **all the VAT on charges paid for the rental of the car under the leasing agreement**, including optional services **unless supplied and identified separately on the tax invoice**, and including an excess mileage charge that forms part of the leasing supply. **Maintenance supplied and invoiced as a separate supply escapes the block** and its VAT is recoverable in full (subject to normal rules). An early-termination charge is caught by the block (from 1 April 2022).

- **Source:** *Motoring expenses (VAT Notice 700/64)* - "You cannot normally recover 50% of the VAT charged. The 50% block is to cover the private use of the car. You can reclaim the remaining 50% of the VAT charged, subject to the normal rules." "The 50% block applies to all the VAT on charges you pay for the rental of the car under the terms of the leasing agreement. This includes: optional services - unless they're supplied and identified separately from the leasing supply on the tax invoice; excess mileage charge - if it forms part of a supply of leasing but not if it was incurred on an excess mileage charge that forms part of a separate supply of maintenance". https://www.gov.uk/guidance/vat-on-motoring-expenses-notice-70064
- **Statutory hook:** *Value Added Tax (Input Tax) Order 1992 (SI 1992/3222) art. 7(1)* blocks tax on "the supply (**including a letting on hire**)" of a motor car; the 50% recovery is the partial relaxation operated under art. 7. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1992/3222/article/7

**Confidence: LOCKED on the 50% rule and its scope (Notice 700/64, primary HMRC practice). UNCONFIRMED on the precise statutory sub-article** delivering the 50% figure: I did not isolate the amending article/paragraph number. **Pages must cite Notice 700/64 and art. 7 generally, and must NOT quote a specific sub-article number for the 50% restriction.**

### 4.4 Electric cars

**Locked position, VAT on purchase.** An electric car is still a **car**. The art. 7 block applies in exactly the same way; there is **no VAT advantage on buying an EV**. The definition in Notice 700/64 is propulsion-neutral (3+ wheels, normally used on public roads, mainly for carrying passengers).

**Locked position, VAT on charging.** Recoverable on **business use** where charging happens **at work or at public charging premises**. A **sole trader or partner** may also recover the business proportion of **home** charging. For an **employee charging at home the employer cannot recover**, because the supply of electricity is made to the employee, not the employer. Mileage records are required to split business and private.

- **Source:** *Motoring expenses (VAT Notice 700/64)* - "VAT incurred by businesses when charging electric vehicles can be recovered on the business use of those vehicles. This applies where the vehicles are charged either: at work; at a public charging premises"; "You can also recover the VAT for charging your electric vehicle for business purposes at home, if you're a: sole proprietor; partner in a partnership business"; for employees charging at home, "The overall supply of electricity is made to the employee and not the employer. The employer is not entitled to recover the VAT on the cost of charging the electric vehicle."; "The employer must keep detailed mileage records". https://www.gov.uk/guidance/vat-on-motoring-expenses-notice-70064

**Locked position, company car benefit in kind (zero-emission).** The appropriate percentage for a **0g/km car is 4% for 2026/27** (3% for 2025/26). Scheduled: **5% for 2027/28**, then **18% for 2028/29** and **19% for 2029/30**.

- **Source:** gov.uk, *Work out the appropriate percentage for company car benefits (480: Appendix 2)* - zero CO2 emissions: **2025-26 = 3%, 2026-27 = 4%**. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/company-car-benefit-the-appropriate-percentage-480-appendix-2
- **Source (later years):** gov.uk policy paper, *Taxation of company cars: The appropriate percentage for tax years 2028 to 2029 and 2029 to 2030* - zero-emission **18% (2028-29)** and **19% (2029-30)**, announced Autumn Budget 2024, "Legislation will be introduced in Finance Bill 2024-25". https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/income-tax-company-car-tax-rates-2028-to-2030/taxation-of-company-cars-the-appropriate-percentage-for-tax-years-2028-to-2029-and-2029-to-2030

**Confidence:** **LOCKED** for **2026/27 = 4%** (Appendix 2, HMRC's live ready reckoner). **LOCKED** for 2025/26 = 3%. **UNCONFIRMED as enacted** for 2027/28 (5%), 2028/29 (18%) and 2029/30 (19%): the 2027/28 figure was not read cleanly off Appendix 2, and the 2028-30 policy paper is written in the future tense ("Legislation will be introduced in Finance Bill 2024-25") and I did **not** verify the corresponding ITEPA 2003 s.139 amendment on legislation.gov.uk. **Writing rule: state 4% for 2026/27 as fact; describe 2027/28 onward as "announced increases, rising steeply from April 2028" and do not present the 18%/19% figures as settled law without a further legislation.gov.uk check.**

### 4.5 VAT on company cars and fuel scale charges

**Locked position.** The art. 7 block applies to a company car exactly as to any other car: no input tax on purchase unless the car is unavailable for private use, 50% on a lease. **Repairs and maintenance VAT is recoverable in full** where the vehicle is used for business, regardless of private motoring. Where a business buys road fuel that is put to private use, it may recover **all** the VAT on road fuel and account for output tax by the **road fuel scale charge**, a flat rate set by the car's **CO2 emissions** (rounded down to the next multiple of 5) and the length of the VAT accounting period. The scale charge is **all-or-nothing across the fleet**: choose it and you must use it for every car in which business fuel is made available for private use.

- **Source:** *Motoring expenses (VAT Notice 700/64)* - "A scale charge is a way of accounting for output tax on road fuel bought by a business for cars that is then put to private use. If you use the scale charge, you can recover all the VAT charged on road fuel without having to split your mileage between business and private use. The charge is worked out on a flat rate basis according to the carbon dioxide emissions of the car."; "Where the CO2 emissions figure is not a multiple of 5, the figure is rounded down to the next multiple of 5"; "If you opt to use the scale charge you must use it for all cars in which your business fuel is made available for private use." https://www.gov.uk/guidance/vat-on-motoring-expenses-notice-70064
- **Source:** gov.uk, *VAT road fuel scale charges* table - charges are stated **only** by CO2 emissions band for petrol and diesel vehicles. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/vat-road-fuel-scale-charges-from-1-may-2025-to-30-april-2026

**Confidence:** **LOCKED** on the block, repairs, and the scale-charge mechanics. **UNCONFIRMED** on the specific question "does a scale charge apply to a fully electric car": the fuel scale charge tables make no mention of electricity or electric vehicles, which strongly implies no, but **HMRC does not say so expressly on either page I fetched**. **Do not assert "there is no fuel scale charge for EVs" on a page.** Say the scale charge is set by CO2 emissions and the published tables cover petrol and diesel, and route the reader to HMRC.

## 5. Household employer / nanny tax (pillar, 3,070/mo, plus a calculator)

### 5.1 PAYE registration trigger

**Locked position.** A household employing a nanny is an **employer** and must register for PAYE with HMRC **before the first payday** if **any** of the following applies to the employee in the current tax year: they are paid **£96 or more a week**, they get **expenses or benefits**, they are **getting a pension**, they have **had another job**, or they have received Jobseeker's Allowance, Employment and Support Allowance or Incapacity Benefit. Registration cannot be done more than 2 months before the first payment. Even where registration is not required, **payroll records must still be kept**.

- **Source:** gov.uk, *PAYE and payroll for employers* - "You must register for PAYE if any of the following applies to an employee in the current tax year (since 6 April): they're paid £96 or more a week; they get expenses and company benefits; they're getting a pension; they've had another job; they've received Jobseeker's Allowance, Employment and Support Allowance or Incapacity Benefit." "If you do not need to register, you'll still need to keep payroll records." https://www.gov.uk/paye-for-employers
- **Source:** gov.uk, *Employing someone to work in your home* - the household employer must "set up and run payroll, or pay someone else to do it on your behalf (even if you pay the employee in cash)" and "deduct and pay the employee's Income Tax and National Insurance contributions". https://www.gov.uk/au-pairs-employment-law
- **Source:** gov.uk, *Register as an employer* - register "when you start employing staff", "before the first payday to get your employer PAYE reference number", and "You cannot register more than 2 months before you start paying people." https://www.gov.uk/register-employer

**Confidence: LOCKED, with a WARNING.** **The registration trigger on gov.uk is £96 a week, which is the 2026/27 SECONDARY threshold (£5,000/yr), NOT the Lower Earnings Limit (£129/wk, £6,708/yr).** Almost every nanny-tax summary states the trigger as "the LEL". On the page HMRC actually publishes today, it is £96. **The calculator and the pillar page must use £96/week as the registration trigger and must not describe it as the LEL.** The LEL matters for a different reason: it is the point at which the employee accrues contributory benefit and state pension entitlement.

### 5.2 2026/27 NIC figures

**Locked position (2026/27, from 6 April 2026):**

| Item | 2026/27 |
|---|---|
| Lower Earnings Limit | **£129/week, £559/month, £6,708/year** |
| Primary threshold (employee) | **£242/week, £1,048/month, £12,570/year** |
| Secondary threshold (employer) | **£96/week, £417/month, £5,000/year** |
| Employee Class 1 rate | **8%** to UEL, then 2% |
| Employer (secondary Class 1) rate | **15%** |
| Employment Allowance | **£10,500** |

- **Source:** gov.uk, *Rates and thresholds for employers 2026 to 2027*. https://www.gov.uk/guidance/rates-and-thresholds-for-employers-2026-to-2027

**Confidence: LOCKED. CONTRADICTS EXISTING HP on the LEL for current-year use.**

house_positions.md line 3 states: "**LEL resolved at £6,500/yr for 2025/26 (the dentists HP £6,708 is the stale one, back-patch queued)**", and §4 and §9 both carry "**Lower Earnings Limit is £6,500/year (£125/week)**".

**Which is right:** both are, for their own year. **£6,500 (£125/wk) is correct for 2025/26. £6,708 (£129/wk) is correct for 2026/27**, the current year. The dentists figure of £6,708 was **not stale, it was early** - it is now the live figure, and the "back-patch queued" note in house_positions is chasing the wrong direction. **Every generalist page written now must use £6,708 / £129 a week, and the house_positions line 3 remark should be corrected at the lock gate.** Employer NIC 15% and the £5,000 secondary threshold are **CONFIRMED unchanged into 2026/27**, so house_positions §4 and §9 are right on those.

### 5.3 Employment Allowance for household employers - CRITICAL

**Locked position.** A person employing a **nanny or other domestic staff cannot claim the Employment Allowance**. Secondary Class 1 liabilities incurred for an employee employed "for purposes connected with the employer's personal, family or household affairs" are **excluded liabilities** by statute. The **only** carve-out is the **care or support worker** exception: the exclusion does not bite where **all** the duties relating to the employer's personal, family or household affairs are performed for an individual who needs care because of old age, disability, past or present alcohol or drug dependence, past or present illness, or past or present mental disorder.

- **Source:** *National Insurance Contributions Act 2014*, **s.2**. s.2(3): "**Liabilities to pay secondary Class 1 contributions incurred by a person ('P') are 'excluded liabilities' if they are incurred in respect of an employed earner who is employed (wholly or partly) for purposes connected with P's personal, family or household affairs.**" s.2(3A) (inserted with effect 6.4.2015) disapplies that exclusion where all such duties are performed for an individual needing care for the listed reasons. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2014/7/section/2
- **Source:** HMRC *National Insurance Manual* **NIM06520 "Employment Allowance: care and support workers"** - "**the Employment Allowance cannot be claimed by someone employing a nanny, unless the nanny is employed solely to care for an individual who needs care for one of the reasons contained at items (a) to (e) above**"; the same restriction extends to gardeners and chauffeurs; where the carve-out applies, "the employing person may claim the Employment Allowance against those secondary Class 1 NICs liabilities, for so long as the person receiving the care needs that care." https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/national-insurance-manual/nim06520

**Confidence: LOCKED. This is the second fact typical summaries get wrong.** Plenty of nanny-payroll marketing says a family "can claim the £10,500 Employment Allowance". For an ordinary nanny employment that is **false**, and the practical consequence is real money: employer NIC at 15% on everything above £5,000 a year is a cost the family bears in full. The **narrow** exception is genuine care work for a person needing care (a live-in carer for an elderly or disabled family member), and the statutory condition is that **all** the personal/family/household duties are performed for that person - a nanny who also childminds a healthy sibling falls outside it.

### 5.4 Can a nanny be self-employed?

**Locked position.** **No, not as a matter of the family's choice.** gov.uk states flatly that an employer of someone working in their home "cannot ask your employee to become self-employed". Status is determined on the ordinary case-law tests, and a nanny working in the family's home, to the family's hours and direction, using the family's equipment, with no business risk, is an employee. A genuinely self-employed childcarer (for example a registered childminder working from their own premises for multiple families) is a different arrangement.

- **Source:** gov.uk, *Employing someone to work in your home* - "**You cannot ask your employee to become self-employed.**" https://www.gov.uk/au-pairs-employment-law
- **Status test tooling:** HMRC *Check employment status for tax (CEST)*, https://www.gov.uk/guidance/check-employment-status-for-tax (referenced, not fetched line by line).

**Confidence: LOCKED** on the gov.uk prohibition. **UNCONFIRMED** as to any HMRC manual paragraph dealing specifically with nannies - I did not locate a nanny-specific ESM page. **Do not cite an ESM paragraph number for nannies**; cite the gov.uk household-employer page and the general status factors (house_positions §13).

## 6. Agent vs principal, and disbursements

**Locked position.** A payment can be excluded from the value of your own supply as a **disbursement** only if **all eight** HMRC conditions are met. If any fails, the payment is a **recharge**: part of the consideration for your own supply, standard-rated if your supply is. You must also be able to prove you **did not claim input tax** on the disbursed payment, which means keeping **separate records** for disbursements. In practice the deciding question is whether the third party's supply was genuinely made **to the client**, or made to you and then used in making your own supply to the client.

The eight conditions, verbatim:
1. "the person acted as an agent of his client when he paid the third party"
2. "the client and not the agent used the goods and services supplied by the third party"
3. "the client was responsible for paying the third party"
4. "the agent was authorised by his client to pay the third party on his behalf"
5. "the client knew that the goods or services were to be provided to him by a third party"
6. "the agent's outlay is separately itemised when he invoices the client"
7. "the amount recovered from the client is exactly the same amount as paid to the third party"
8. "the goods or services paid for by the agent are clearly additional to the agent's own supplies"

- **Source:** HMRC *VAT Taxable Person Manual* **VTAXPER39000 "Issues to consider: agency and disbursements: how to recognise a disbursement - the eight conditions"**. Also: "He must also be able to prove that he did not claim input tax on that payment. This will involve keeping separate records for disbursements." https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/vat-taxable-person/vtaxper39000
- **Statutory hook (agency):** VATA 1994 **s.47** (agents; s.47(2A) and s.47(3), disclosed and undisclosed agents), covered at VTAXPER37820 and VTAXPER37900 (identified, not fetched).

**Confidence: LOCKED on the eight conditions.** **UNCONFIRMED:** VAT Notice 700 section 25 (the public-facing version of the same test) was **not** successfully fetched - the notice page truncated at section 14. Cite **VTAXPER39000** as the source in copy, not "Notice 700 section 25", unless someone re-fetches the notice. The VATA 1994 s.47 text itself was also not fetched; do not quote it.

**No existing house_positions section covers this. New anchor, no contradiction.**

## 7. Rent a chair (hairdressing)

**Locked position.** Chair rental by a hairdressing salon to a self-employed stylist is **standard rated, not exempt**. A specific statutory exclusion pulls it out of the land exemption: the grant of facilities to a person who uses them wholly or mainly to supply hairdressing services is excluded from Schedule 9 Group 1 exemption. It falls back into exemption **only** where the grant is of a **clearly demarcated area** (an entire building, floor, or defined area) **with no related hairdressing services** supplied with it. Where the salon also supplies assistants, reception, appointment booking, towel laundering, washbasins or a client waiting area, those are **not ancillary to a licence to occupy** but an integral part of a single taxable supply of facilities.

- **Source:** *Value Added Tax Act 1994*, **Schedule 9, Group 1 (Land), Item 1, paragraph (ma)**: "**the grant of facilities to a person who uses the facilities wholly or mainly to supply hairdressing services**" (excluded from exemption), with the accompanying Notes restoring exemption where the grant is of exclusive use of a whole building, floor or defined area without related hairdressing services. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1994/23/schedule/9
- **Source:** HMRC *VAT Land and Property Manual* **VATLP19820 "Hairdressing salons - chair rentals: what are 'chair rentals'?"** - chair rentals include "a chair with certain rights of access or a clearly defined area" together with "services related to hairdressing" such as assistants, appointment booking and towel laundering; "**When a hairdressing salon rents chair spaces to individual self-employed stylists, the salon's supplies to the individual stylists will be taxable.**" https://www.gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/vat-land-and-property/vatlp19820

**Confidence: LOCKED.** Related manual pages exist at VATLP19800 (contents), VATLP19810 (historic position) and VATLP19830 (pre-legislation case law), and VTAXPER68900/69100 deal with the separate, prior question of **to whom the stylist supplies** (salon or customer), which drives whether the stylist's own turnover counts toward their own £90,000 registration threshold. Those were identified but **not fetched line by line**; do not quote them.

**No existing house_positions section covers this. New anchor, no contradiction.**
